prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Grandma is washing me white. I am the color of hot sand in the bleached sea light. I am a stain on the porcelain, persistent as tea. Stay in the shade. Don’t say she was the only one. Cousins opposite say: you too white. I am a night-blooming flower being pried open in the morning. My skin a curtain for a cage of bones, a blackbird coop. My heart is crusty bread, hardening. Hardening. This way, I feed my own fluttering. Under shade, the day looks like evening and I cannot bear the darkness. Don’t say, I can’t stand to be touched. Say, I stare into the sun to burn off the soiled hands that print my body with bloody ink. Don’t say, Mulatto. Say, I am the horse in Oz turning different colors, each prance brightening flesh. A curiosity. Don’t say, Bathwater spiraled down into the pipes. Say, I never did fade. Say, Skin holds the perseverance of my days. Folding, folding, the water continuously gathers, making wrinkles in a map.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker describes a painful struggle with colorism, feeling judged as both too dark and too white.
- The grandmother’s attempt to “wash” the speaker white symbolizes pressure to erase or alter the speaker’s racial identity.
- Images of darkness, hardening, and unwanted touch convey emotional pain, isolation, and bodily trauma.
- The speaker rejects dehumanizing labels and reframes shifting skin color as vivid, resilient, and impossible to erase.
- In the end, skin becomes a lasting record of survival, preserving the perseverance and history of the speaker’s life.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Grandma, Stay, Don

outputs.L1:
Grandma is washing me white. I am the color of hot sand beneath bleached sea light. I am a stain on porcelain, as persistent as tea. Stay in the shade. Don’t say she was the only one. Cousins across from me say: You’re too white.

I am a night-blooming flower pried open in the morning. My skin is a curtain drawn over a cage of bones, a blackbird coop. My heart is crusty bread, hardening. Hardening. In this way, I feed my own fluttering.

Beneath the shade, day looks like evening, and I cannot bear the darkness. Don’t say: I can’t stand to be touched. Say: I stare into the sun to burn away the soiled hands that print my body in bloody ink.

Don’t say: Mulatto. Say: I am the horse in Oz, turning different colors, each prance brightening my flesh. A curiosity.

Don’t say: Bathwater spiraled down into the pipes. Say: I never did fade. Say: Skin holds the perseverance of my days. Folding, folding, the water gathers continuously, making wrinkles in a map.
outputs.L2: Grandmother scrubs me toward whiteness. Beneath the sea’s washed-out glare, my body carries the shade of sun-scorched sand. Against porcelain, I linger like the brown trace tea refuses to surrender. Keep out of the sunlight. Do not claim she acted alone. Across from me, my cousins insist that I am also too pale. I am a blossom meant for midnight, forced apart at dawn. My skin drapes over its enclosure of bone, an aviary holding a dark bird. My heart resembles a loaf gone stale, its crust growing firmer and firmer. From that hardness, I nourish the wings beating inside me. In shadow, afternoon resembles dusk, yet I cannot endure the dimness. Do not say that touch repels me. Say instead that I look straight at the sun, hoping its fire will erase the defiling handprints stamped across my body in blood-colored ink. Do not call me “Mulatto.” Call me the color-changing horse from Oz, every step transforming and illuminating its flesh—something displayed as a wonder. Do not say the bathwater twisted away through the plumbing. Say that my color never disappeared. Say that skin preserves the endurance of everything I have survived. Again and again it creases, while water keeps collecting and drawing wrinkles across a map.
outputs.L3:
The speaker describes a painful struggle with colorism and racial identity, feeling judged from conflicting directions—as both too dark and too white. This contradiction suggests that the speaker is denied the freedom to define their own identity, instead being measured against other people’s expectations of what their skin color should represent. The grandmother’s attempt to “wash” the speaker white becomes a powerful symbol of this pressure. Rather than simply describing a physical act, the image reveals an effort to erase, alter, or make the speaker’s racial identity more socially acceptable.

Throughout the work, images of darkness, hardening, and unwanted touch communicate deep emotional and physical suffering. Darkness reflects isolation and rejection, while hardening suggests the defenses the speaker has developed in response to repeated harm. References to touch also emphasize that prejudice is not merely an abstract judgment; it is experienced through the body, leaving lasting emotional and traumatic effects.

Despite this pain, the speaker refuses the labels and attitudes that attempt to dehumanize them. Instead, shifting skin color is reimagined as vivid, adaptable, and resilient. What others treat as a source of shame becomes evidence of strength—something that cannot be washed away or erased. By the end, skin functions as a permanent record of survival. It carries the marks of hardship, but it also preserves the speaker’s perseverance, identity, and personal history. The body therefore becomes not an object to be corrected, but a living archive of everything the speaker has endured and overcome.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores the intertwined effects of colorism, racial ambiguity, and bodily violation, showing how the speaker’s skin becomes a site of judgment, control, and resistance. Images of washing and fading suggest repeated attempts to cleanse, lighten, or erase an identity that others find difficult to categorize or accept. References to shade and shifting skin color further emphasize the instability of racial perception: the speaker’s body is interpreted differently depending on light, context, and the prejudices of those looking at it. In this way, color is not presented as a neutral physical trait but as something burdened by social hierarchies and expectations.

The poem’s imagery of touch adds a more intimate and disturbing dimension to this conflict. The body is not only observed but also handled, tested, and violated, revealing how racial scrutiny can become physically invasive. Such contact threatens the speaker’s autonomy by treating the skin as an object available for examination or possession. Yet the body also preserves the evidence of what it has endured. Rather than becoming blank or purified through washing, the skin functions as a living record of harm, memory, ancestry, and survival.

Ultimately, the poem rejects the possibility that the speaker can be erased. Although skin may appear to change across different conditions, the self beneath those shifting perceptions remains intact. The refusal to be “faded” transforms the poem’s recurring imagery into a declaration of resilience. What others attempt to diminish becomes the very source of the speaker’s strength: the skin carries identity forward, bearing witness to violation while refusing to surrender its history or meaning.
outputs.L5:
Grandma asked Don to stay a little longer. The evening had grown quiet, and rain tapped softly against the kitchen window. Don looked at the clock, then at the warm cup of tea she had poured for him.

“Just one more story,” Grandma said with a smile.

So Don stayed. As she spoke about her childhood, the old house seemed to fill with life again. By the time the rain stopped, Don understood that staying had not cost him an evening—it had given him a memory he would carry forever.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about a mixed-race speaker whose grandmother tries to wash their skin lighter, exploring colorism, bodily autonomy, family judgment, and resilience through surreal imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
My grandmother fills the basin with milk and moonlight, says, Come here, child, let me help you.

Her hands smell of lye soap, gardenias, and the old country’s fear. She scrubs my shoulders as if dusk were a stain, as if my father’s blood were mud tracked across her clean floor. In the water, small brown planets loosen from me and refuse to drown. They orbit her wrists. They whisper my name.

Hold still, she says. Beauty requires patience.

But my skin is not a curtain she can bleach until the neighbors stop staring. It is an orchard grafted from two histories, bearing fruit no one in the family knows how to name. At dinner, the spoons tilt toward me like tiny silver judges. An aunt pinches my cheek and calls me almost pretty. A cousin praises winter for making me pale. Each word enters my body wearing a white glove.

Grandmother scrubs harder.

The bathroom walls grow mouths. The mirror puts on a judge’s wig. Even the towels hiss, Choose a side.

I look down and see continents moving beneath my skin—rivers braiding, borders dissolving, ancestors lifting their faces through mine. One carries a drum. One carries a hymn. One carries nothing but the stubborn flame of having survived.

Enough, I say.

The word is small, but it cracks the basin. Milk floods the floor. Moonlight climbs the walls. The soap turns into a pale moth and beats itself senseless against the bulb.

I take my arm back.

Grandmother’s face folds like a letter she has been afraid to open. For a moment, I see the child she was, powdered and warned, taught to fear the sun inside herself. I love her then—not as surrender, not as permission, but as one loves a wounded animal without offering it another body to bite.

I step from the water wearing every shade I was given.

Behind me, the family gathers its scales, its charts, its careful jars of acceptable light. Let them measure. Let them murmur. My body is not a family vote.

Outside, night opens its dark, unwashed hands.

I place mine inside.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental first-person poem using repeated phrases like “Don’t say” and “Say.” Center it on skin, racial identity, unwanted touch, bathwater, shade, and the refusal to fade.
counterfactuals.output:
**UNFADE**

Don’t say *beautiful*  
with your hand already reaching.

Say: *May I?*  
Say it before the border,  
before my skin becomes  
a country you enter  
without papers.

Don’t say *I don’t see color.*

I have spent whole summers  
being translated by light.  
I have watched bathwater brown  
around my knees—  
dust, blood, street, history—  
and still stepped out  
the same shade of myself.

Say: *I see you.*

Don’t say *exotic.*  
Don’t say *almost white.*  
Don’t say *dark, but not too dark.*  
Don’t arrange my face  
on your little wheel of permission.

Say: *Your name.*  
Say: *Your name again.*  
Say it until you stop trying  
to rename the weather.

In the tub, I sink  
until only my mouth survives.

The water keeps touching me,  
but water knows how to leave.

Your fingers did not.

Don’t say *it was nothing.*  
Nothing does not linger  
on the shoulder.  
Nothing does not bloom  
into flinch.

Say: *I was wrong.*

My skin is not a question  
you can answer with your palm.  
My skin is not proof  
for whichever story  
makes you innocent.

Don’t say *fade.*  
Don’t say *blend.*  
Don’t say *give it time.*

I have given time enough:  
to bleach, to shadow,  
to mirrors lit like interrogations,  
to family photographs  
where every generation  
stands in a different sun.

Say: *shade.*

Say: *inheritance.*

Say: *the body remembers  
what the mouth edits.*

I rise from the bath,  
water breaking from me  
in bright, temporary rivers.

Look—

the towel takes the wet,  
the night takes the window,  
the years take what they can.

Don’t say I disappeared.

Say I remained.

Say I remain.

Say my skin, my skin, my skin—

and keep your hands  
to yourself.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dense, image-rich prose poem about a biracial person remembering childhood bathing rituals and relatives commenting that they are “too white.” Include references to porcelain stains, blackbirds, bread, flowers, and The Wizard of Oz.
counterfactuals.output:
In the blue hour of the bathroom, my mother lowered me into the tub as if returning a moon to water. The porcelain wore its rust-colored stains like old countries on a map—continents no bleach could conquer—and around my knees the soap opened its white flowers, petal after petal, until my brown skin blurred beneath them. She scrubbed behind my ears with a washcloth warm as bread, saying hush, hush, while steam softened the mirror and made us both ghosts.

Later, in the kitchen, relatives pinched my wrist beneath the yellow light. Too white, they said, laughing, though the words landed like blackbirds along a telephone wire, each one facing the same cold direction. Too white to tan right, too white to know the songs, too white until I burned, until I vanished against winter, until somebody mentioned the other half of me and everyone chewed their bread.

I remember bath nights by their weather: my grandmother’s lavender soap; my father’s dark arm testing the water; the garden outside, where marigolds kept their little fires alive. I remember thinking color must be something that rinsed off, something circling the drain with shampoo and dead skin. If I stayed under long enough, perhaps I would rise unmistakable—ruby-slipper certain, Technicolor whole.

But childhood was always Kansas turning into Oz: one door opened and the world accused you of becoming vivid. In the mirror’s fog I drew a face, then wiped it away. Beyond the window, blackbirds lifted from the lawn like thrown ink. My mother wrapped me in a towel, and I smelled of rain, flour, flowers crushed underfoot. Too white, the house murmured. Too much. Not enough.

Still, she carried me down the hallway, my wet hair dripping a bright road behind us, and for one small, shining minute I belonged entirely to her arms—the way bread belongs to hunger, the way a stain belongs to porcelain, the way every lost child belongs to the impossible green light of home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a haunting monologue in which washing becomes a metaphor for erasure, trauma, and colorism. Use fragmented sentences, repetition, and transformations of painful statements into defiant ones.
counterfactuals.output:
Wash, they said.

Wash your face.  
Wash your hands.  
Wash that darkness from your knees, your elbows, the soft brown moons beneath your eyes.

As if darkness were dirt.  
As if I had been careless with myself.

So I scrubbed.

Soap under my nails.  
Bleach-scent in the throat.  
Water running gray, then clear, then gray again—because memory does not rinse clean. Because the body keeps what the mouth is forbidden to name.

Too dark, they said.

Too dark for the photograph.  
Too dark for the dress.  
Too dark to be delicate.  
Too dark to be chosen.

I learned to stand beneath hard light and disappear.

Wash, they said.

And I washed the hand from my shoulder.  
Washed the locked door.  
Washed the voice that told me hush.  
Washed until my skin burned bright with the proof of trying.

But pain is waterproof.

It beads.  
It waits.  
It enters through the cracks.

For years, I mistook erasure for healing. I called the rawness clean. I called the silence peace. I called myself almost beautiful when they meant almost pale.

Almost.  
Almost.  
Almost gone.

Too dark, they said.

Now I say: dark enough to hold the night without breaking.

Too much, they said.

Now I say: enough to flood every room that tried to contain me.

Dirty, they said.

No.

Marked.

Marked by survival. Marked by hands that failed to finish the sentence of me. Marked by a history that wanted my color diluted, softened, corrected.

No.

I will not be corrected.

Let the basin fill. Let the mirror cloud. Let every cruel word loosen from my body and circle the drain—not my skin, not my name, not the deep earth of my face.

I am done washing myself away.

I wash now to return.

To return the shame to its speaker.  
To return the fear to the locked room.  
To return the lie to the mouth that made it.

The water runs.

Not clear.

Never clear.

Brown with soil. Red with remembering. Gold where the light finds me.

Beautiful, I say.

Beautiful.

And this time, the mirror does not argue.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a surreal literary poem about mixed-race embodiment and survival, contrasting darkness and bleaching, touch and resistance, fading and perseverance. End with water gathering into wrinkles like a map.
counterfactuals.output:
My body was born at the border of two mirrors,  
each insisting the other was night.  
In one, my mother’s hands braided thunder;  
in the other, my father’s silence  
wore a pale, borrowed sun.

They called darkness a room without doors,  
then sold us bleach in little moons—  
promises that stung the tongue,  
that whitened the towels,  
that could not erase the drum beneath the skin.

I learned touch as both weather and warning:  
a palm could bless the cheek,  
a finger could inventory it.  
Strangers reached for my hair  
as if survival were public property.

So I grew thorns inward, carefully,  
leaving the surface soft enough for love.  
I became the animal that sleeps through fire,  
the seed rehearsing green  
under a century of ash.

Some days I fade at the edges—  
photograph, shoreline, unclaimed name—  
but fading is not disappearance.  
Even dusk keeps its red blade.  
Even paper remembers the forest.

I carry my divided ancestors  
not as halves, but as doors  
opening into one another.  
Behind them, the dead are washing their faces,  
refusing every soap that calls them stain.

And I remain: salt-dark, scar-bright,  
a vessel cracked into greater capacity,  
holding every touch I resisted,  
every touch that taught me to stay,  
until water gathers into my wrinkles like a map.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
